name: Castor oil
short: By mouth: 5 of 8 ill newborns given castor oil tea died; amniotic fluid embolism, uterine rupture at term (cases). Eye: review, corneal cell death in 100; trial, no drop-related complications in 20.
text: This entry covers castor oil put into the eye (eye drops or emulsion drops); data for castor oil applied to the eyelids or taken by mouth are labelled as such and do not describe eye drops. In the eye: a 2007 cosmetic-ingredient safety review summarises two human studies of castor oil instilled into the eye: in nine patients, a castor oil solution caused mild and transient discomfort and minor changes to the eye's surface cells, and in a study of 100 patients, instilled castor oil caused death of corneal surface (epithelial) cells and breaks in that surface layer (the abstract does not give the concentrations used). In a randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 20 patients (40 eyes) with meibomian gland dysfunction, eye drops of 2% castor oil with 5% polyoxyethylene castor oil as an emulsifier, used six times a day for 2 weeks, were followed by no observed complications attributable to the drops. In a survey of 283 people with corneal ulcers at an eye hospital in South India, 135 had used traditional eye medicines, castor oil among them in 16; the abstract does not say whether the remedies caused the ulcers. On the eyelids (a different route, not drops): in a 4-week randomised paired-eye trial in 26 people with blepharitis, 100% cold-pressed castor oil applied to the eyelids twice daily caused no reported adverse events. By mouth (a different route; these data do not describe eye drops): in a neonatal unit in Haiti, eight newborns among 1,424 admissions over 2 years had an illness resembling sepsis, with shock, vomiting, floppiness (hypotonia), lethargy and a swollen abdomen; five died and a sixth left hospital close to death. In each case the illness was associated with having been given teas that included castor oil, and caregivers said the infants had been given large amounts (a case series; the authors call the tea the presumptive cause). A case report describes an amniotic fluid embolism causing cardiorespiratory arrest, temporally associated with castor oil taken at term in a normal pregnancy, in a woman without the usual risk factors. Another case report describes a woman at 39 weeks with a previous caesarean who had severe abdominal pain and rupture of membranes shortly after taking castor oil; a caesarean 45 minutes later, prompted by repetitive variable decelerations (dips in the baby's heart rate), found the umbilical cord protruding through a 2-cm rupture of the old caesarean scar. Used to start labour: in a Cochrane review of three trials (233 women), all women who took castor oil felt nauseous; caesarean rates did not differ significantly in the two trials that reported them (risk ratio 2.04, 95% CI 0.92 to 4.55), there was no evidence of a difference from placebo or no treatment in meconium-stained fluid or in low Apgar scores at five minutes, the trials were too small to detect all but large differences, and no data were given on deaths or illness in mothers or babies; the authors say the results should be interpreted with caution because of poor methodological quality. Another systematic review of trials found a tendency towards more caesarean sections and meconium-stained amniotic fluid (the baby's first stool released into the fluid around it). In a retrospective descriptive study at one birth centre, maternal adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting or extreme diarrhoea occurred in less than 7% of 323 women given a castor oil cocktail (the abstract does not list the cocktail's other ingredients), with adverse effects of any kind in less than 15% of births, and a meta-analysis of 12 studies (1653 pregnant women) found that none reported serious harmful effects. The safety review notes that castor oil does not contain ricin, the poison in the castor seed. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
